- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.10) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast by 1–3% for next period.
- When sentiment is negative (≤-0.15) and prices are trending down, model often underestimates; increase forecast by 1–3% to account for mean reversion.
- After a sharp price spike (≥5% from prior peak), model frequently overshoots in subsequent days; apply a 2–5% downward correction to avoid overreaction.
- If model forecast is significantly above true outcome (e.g., >5% higher), check sentiment for bullish bias — if sentiment is weak or neutral, reduce forecast to align with recent mean.
- If model forecast is consistently below true outcome (e.g., >5% lower), sentiment may be bearish — if sentiment turns positive, increase forecast by 1–2% to capture momentum.
- For 30-day horizon, model often fails to capture late-period momentum; adjust final 5–7 days of forecast upward if sentiment turns bullish or price shows upward momentum.
- If sentiment history shows repeated negative spikes (e.g., -0.28, -0.22), model tends to underestimate — apply a 2–4% upward bias to correct for sentiment-driven underreaction.
- Model often overreacts to short-term sentiment shifts — if sentiment changes direction within 3–5 days, adjust forecast to reflect gradual reversion, not abrupt reversal.
